specPoints.text: understand that the growth of the pollen tube followed by fertilisation leads to seed and fruit formation

primer.text: Pollination only parks the pollen; fertilisation finishes the journey. This note follows the pollen tube down the style to the ovary, watches the two nuclei fuse into a zygote, and then tracks the aftermath — the ovule swelling into a seed while the flower around it becomes the fruit that disperses it.

lessons.title: Pollen Tube to Zygote
lessons.opening: After pollination succeeds, the pollen grain grows a tube down the style toward the ovary; the pollen nucleus travels that tube and fuses with the ovum nucleus, forming the zygote where fertilisation is complete.
keyPoints: Once pollination lands pollen on the stigma, the grain grows a tube that carries its male nucleus toward the ovary.
The tube grows down the style toward the ovary.
The pollen nucleus travels down the pollen tube.
Fertilisation completes when pollen nucleus and ovum nucleus merge into a single zygote.

low.restatement: The pollen drills a tunnel down the style and its nucleus rides it to the egg cell for the fusion.
low.analogy: A miner digging a shaft so the payloader can reach the vault.
low.examPointer: Keep pollination and fertilisation separate — landing versus fusing.

medium.restatement: The tube exists because pollen cannot move itself through tissue; its growth is the delivery system, and only the nucleus makes the trip, meeting the ovum deep in the ovary for the fusion that starts the new plant.
medium.analogy: A train laid to a station so the passenger can board.
medium.examPointer: Name the two nuclei that fuse — pollen nucleus and ovum nucleus — in the definition.

check.stem: What forms after successful pollination to reach the ovum?

options.text: A pollen tube growing from the pollen grain
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The style already exists; the tube grows through it.
The ovary is a flower part, not a tube product.
Seeds form after fertilisation, not at pollination.

check.stem: Along which route does the pollen tube grow?

options.text: Down the style toward the ovary
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Up the stigma into the air
options.explanation: The tube grows inward, not outward.

options.text: Along the filament to the anther
options.explanation: The anther is the male part that made the pollen.

options.text: Out of the petal to a pollinator
options.explanation: Pollinators carried the grain; the tube works alone now.

check.stem: What exactly fuses during fertilisation in a flower?

options.text: The pollen nucleus fusing with the ovum nucleus
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The whole pollen grain and the stigma
options.explanation: The stigma only received the grain.
One male nucleus fuses with one female nucleus.
Those are structures, not fusing cells.

check.stem: What single cell results when the two plant nuclei merge?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The tube formed before fusion.
The ovule develops into a seed after fertilisation.
Fruit forms from surrounding flower parts, later.

check.stem: Why must the pollen nucleus travel down a tube rather than swimming to the ovum?

options.text: The route runs through solid style tissue, so the tube delivers the nucleus to the ovary
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Nectar is a reward; there is no swim channel.
Wind was the courier outside; inside the tube does the work.

options.text: The ovum crawls up to meet pollen
options.explanation: The ovum stays put in the ovary.

check.stem: State where the pollen tube grows and what it delivers.
check.modelAnswer: The pollen tube grows down the style and delivers the male nucleus into the ovary.

check.stem: State the definition of fertilisation in plants.
check.modelAnswer: Fertilisation is the moment the pollen nucleus merges with the ovum nucleus, creating a zygote.

check.stem: Explain why pollination and fertilisation are not the same event.
check.modelAnswer: Pollination is pollen landing on the stigma, while fertilisation happens later when the nuclei fuse inside the ovary after the tube's growth.

check.stem: A chemical blocks style tissue growth so no tube can form. Predict the consequence for reproduction.
check.modelAnswer: The pollen nucleus could not reach the ovum, so fertilisation would fail and no seed would form.

lessons.title: Seeds, Fruits and Dispersal
lessons.opening: Fertilisation flips the flower's afterlife: each fertilised ovule swells into a seed, and the flower parts around the ovary develop into a fruit that packages those seeds for dispersal — eaten by animals or hitching rides on fur with sticky hooks.
keyPoints: Once fertilisation is done, the ovule swells into a seed.
The flower parts wrapped around that ovule then grow into a fruit.
The fruit contains the seeds and provides a mechanism for seed dispersal.
Some fruits are eaten by animals, which disperse the seeds in their droppings.
Some fruits carry sticky hooks that catch in the fur of passing animals.

low.restatement: Ovule to seed, flower wall to fruit; the fruit then ships the seeds away.
low.analogy: The seed is the parcel, the fruit is the padded envelope, and animals are the postal service.
low.examPointer: Map the transformations — ovule to seed, surroundings to fruit — in that order.

medium.restatement: Dispersal pays because a seed germinating beside its parent competes with it; animal droppings and hooked fur both move seeds far from the parent plant, spreading the next generation into fresh ground.
medium.analogy: Children moving out of the family home rather than crowding one roof.
medium.examPointer: Give one named dispersal mechanism with its fruit adaptation to score fully.

check.stem: What does the ovule become after fertilisation?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The fruit forms from the surrounding flower parts.
The tube already served its delivery role.
The ovary is where the ovule sat; it does not become one.

check.stem: Which structures develop into the fruit?

options.text: The flower tissues that wrap around the ovule
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Ovules become seeds inside the fruit.
Pollen delivered the male nucleus and is spent.
The surrounding ovary tissues form the fruit wall.

check.stem: Why do fruits help the plant's offspring?

options.text: They provide a mechanism for seed dispersal away from the parent
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They feed the seed while it grows
options.explanation: The seed carries its own food store.

options.text: They attract pollinators to the flower
options.explanation: Pollination already happened.
Fertilisation is complete before fruit growth.

check.stem: A fox eats berries and walks kilometres before its droppings land. What service did the fox provide?

options.text: Seed dispersal, moving the seeds far from the parent plant
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The fox ate fruit, not pollen.
Fertilisation happened in the flower, long before.
Germination starts after dispersal, once deposited.

check.stem: Which fruit adaptation suits hitching a ride on an animal's coat?

options.text: Sticky hooks that catch in fur
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Sweet flesh eaten for the flesh itself
options.explanation: Sweet flesh suits droppings dispersal, not hooks.
Colour attracts eaters; hooks do the attaching.
Stones protect seeds; they do not grip fur.

check.stem: State what the ovule and the surrounding flower parts become after fertilisation.
check.modelAnswer: The ovule becomes a seed, and the flower parts that wrapped it become the fruit.

check.stem: Name two fruit dispersal mechanisms given in the lesson.
check.modelAnswer: Fruits can be eaten by animals that disperse seeds in droppings, or carry sticky hooks that catch in animal fur.

check.stem: Explain why seed dispersal benefits the next generation of plants.
check.modelAnswer: Dispersal moves seeds away from the parent plant, so seedlings do not compete with the parent or with each other for light, water and minerals.

check.stem: A meadow plant makes hooked fruits while a neighbour makes sweet fleshy fruits. Assign each its dispersal agent.
check.modelAnswer: The hooked fruits hitch on passing animals' fur, and the fleshy fruits are eaten by animals that disperse the seeds in their droppings.

glossary.definition: The tube growing from a pollen grain down the style to deliver the male nucleus.
The fusion of the pollen nucleus with the ovum nucleus to form a zygote.
The ovary structure that develops into a seed after fertilisation.
